component.name: BifroSSH
component.summary: GUI SSH client with built-in SFTP and keychain management

description.p: BifroSSH is a modern SSH client with a full terminal emulator, SFTP file browser, SSH key management, per-server theming, and codeprints for quick command access.

ul.li: SFTP file browser with upload, download, and folder navigation
SSH key management with encrypted local keychain
Customisable themes including a built-in theme editor
Codeprints: named commands that can be pasted or run in any session

screenshot.caption: Hosts, with an icon per operating system
Confirming a server's fingerprint on first connection
Browsing files over SFTP, local beside remote
Saved commands in the Codeprints sidebar
Local, remote and SOCKS port forwarding
Editing a host, including its jump host
Exporting a setup to carry to another machine

description.p: Nine of the built-in colour schemes have been renamed after what they look like: Phosphor, Midnight, Deep Slate, Legal Pad, Parchment, Ember, Moss, Graphite and Classic Light. Their colours are unchanged. Two others, Manhattan and Plastic World, have been removed.
A host set to any of those themes goes back to the default and needs picking again. Themes you made yourself are not affected.
The colour schemes contributed by other people are now credited, with their licences, in THIRD_PARTY.md.

A terminal is drawn entirely in the colours of the theme it was given. The border around the edge of the terminal kept the colour of the default theme whichever one was chosen, which showed as a mismatched frame around anything else.
Themes made in the theme editor now apply to sessions. Choosing one for a host showed its name in the host settings, but the session itself was still drawn in the default colours.

A new session no longer loses the first thing it says. The welcome message and opening prompt were being produced before the terminal was ready to receive them, so a connection could look like it had opened to an empty screen until you pressed a key.

Pasting several lines at once behaves the way the program you are pasting into expects. In a shell they arrive as one block you can still edit before running, and in an editor they keep their own indentation instead of stepping further right on every line.

Terminal search, copy and paste keep working on keyboard layouts that do not produce Latin letters. Closing a busy session no longer risks an error, and a terminal no longer briefly redraws itself a moment after connecting.

The terminal can be searched. Ctrl+Shift+F finds text anywhere in the scrollback, highlighting every match with a running count, and steps through them with Enter and Shift+Enter. Matching by case, by whole word or by regular expression can each be turned on. The bar sits over the terminal rather than taking a row from it, so opening it does not disturb a full-screen program running on the far end.

A host with no key, password or prompt authentication set up now says so instead of doing nothing when you connect to it. The reason appears in the connection log alongside every other kind of failure, and the host can be opened for editing from there. A host pointing at an identity that has since been deleted says that specifically.
The first option when right clicking a host reads Connect until a session is open to it, and Duplicate only afterwards.

A setup can now be carried to another machine. Settings writes a single encrypted file holding your hosts, identities, keys, tunnels, codeprints, themes, settings and known hosts, and importing it elsewhere brings all of it across. Copying the data file by hand never worked for this, because it is sealed with a key belonging to the machine it was made on.

The file is protected by a passphrase you choose for it rather than your master key, which is what lets it open somewhere that has never seen this installation. That passphrase is stored nowhere and cannot be recovered, and passwords and private keys can be left out of the file entirely.

Importing only ever adds. Anything already on the machine is kept and reported as skipped, so the same file can be imported twice with no effect and an old export cannot undo newer changes. A server whose host key the file disagrees with is reported and left alone.

A desktop keyring that is locked is no longer mistaken for one that has lost the key. The two look the same from outside and want opposite handling: a locked keyring still holds your key and only needs unlocking, so BifroSSH now says so and leaves it alone, where before it could have replaced a perfectly good copy.
Where the keyring copy really has stopped working, entering your master passphrase repairs it, instead of the passphrase being asked for at every launch from then on with no way back.
Passphrase boxes can now be revealed while typing, which matters most for the generated word phrase, since that one is read back off paper and was the hardest thing here to type unseen.
The unlock screen follows the theme you chose. It could not before, because the theme is kept with the rest of your settings and those cannot be read until the passphrase has been entered.

The key that encrypts your saved passwords and private keys no longer has to sit in a file beside them. On first launch you choose where it is kept: in your desktop keyring with a passphrase to fall back on, or behind a passphrase alone, or in a file as before. All three remain reachable from Settings, which now reports where the key actually is rather than the best place it could be.

Where a passphrase is used, one can be generated for you as eight words. Capitalisation and spacing are ignored when it is typed back, because it is written on paper and read back later, and that is when transcription goes wrong.

The whole of the stored data is encrypted now, not only the credentials, so hostnames, usernames, jump host chains, forwarding rules and saved commands are no longer readable in the file. That file is also written so an interrupted save cannot destroy it, is readable only by your own account, and keeps the previous version alongside it to recover from.
The window is served a Content Security Policy, and the application identifier now matches the one everything else already used.

Packaging only, with no changes to the application itself. Releases are now built, signed and published from a clean checkout rather than from a developer machine, so what is published is reproducible from the tagged source alone.

A server that is not reachable directly can now be reached through a bastion, the same as ssh's ProxyJump. Pick any other saved host as a host's jump host, and chains of them are followed one link at a time.

Every hop is a full connection of its own: it uses its own stored credentials, and its host key is checked and confirmed separately, so a bastion has to be trusted before it can carry anything. Terminal sessions, file transfers and port forwarding all travel the chain.
Hosts that name a jump host in ~/.ssh/config are now linked up on import instead of being flagged as unsupported.

Whole folders can now be transferred over SFTP, in either direction or between two remote servers, instead of only one file at a time. Progress shows which file of how many is moving, and symbolic links are skipped rather than followed.

Existing hosts can be imported from ~/.ssh/config. The dialog lists what was found before anything is created, skips hosts already saved, and references identity files where they are rather than copying private keys.

Sessions and tunnels now send a keepalive, so they survive NAT and firewall idle timers and report a dead host instead of hanging. Each connection also keeps a log of how it was established, reviewable from the session sidebar after the fact.

Port forwarding rules, codeprints and custom themes are now kept with the rest of your data instead of in browser storage, where clearing browsing data destroyed them. Existing entries are migrated automatically on first launch.
Identities can now authenticate using keys held by a running ssh-agent instead of importing the private key into BifroSSH. The agent signs the challenge, so the key never enters the app.

This covers keys already loaded with ssh-add or held by a desktop keyring, and PIV smartcards and YubiKeys in PIV mode, whose keys cannot be exported and so could not be used at all before. Pick a specific key by fingerprint, or let BifroSSH try each key the agent offers. FIDO security keys are not supported yet, but are ignored rather than preventing the other keys in the agent from working.

BifroSSH can now log in to servers that ask challenge questions instead of accepting a stored credential. That covers PAM setups with password authentication turned off, and two-factor providers such as Duo, TOTP authenticator apps and hardware tokens, none of which could be connected to before.

Set an identity's auth mode to Prompt and nothing is stored for it; the server asks and you answer at connect time. Where the server offers a choice of second factors, the options appear as buttons, so approving a push notification takes a single click. Password and key logins fall back to this automatically.

BifroSSH now verifies the host key of every server it connects to, the same way OpenSSH does. The first time you connect to a server you are shown its fingerprint and asked to confirm it; after that the key is remembered and checked on every connection. If a server ever presents a different key, the connection is refused.

Servers already listed in your ~/.ssh/known_hosts are trusted automatically and will not prompt. A new Known Hosts panel lets you review stored fingerprints, choose how unknown servers are handled, and forget individual hosts.
